context.description:
STI Education Systems Holdings, Inc. (STI), formerly JTH Davies Holdings, Inc., was originally established in 1928 as the Philippine branch office of Theo H. Davies & Co., a Hawaiian corporation. The Company was reincorporated as a Philippine corporation registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on June 28, 1946. After many years of operations as part of the Jardine-Matheson group, STI was sold to local Philippine investors in 2006. In March 2010, the Company became part of the Tanco Group of Companies. On September 10, 2012, the SEC approved the change in name to the present one.

STI is the holding company within the Tanco Group that derives investment in its education business. The Company's subsidiaries are STI Education Services Group, Inc. (STI ESG); STI West Negros University, Inc.; iACADEMY, Inc.; and Attenborough Holdings Corporation. STI ESG has a total of 63 schools nationwide.

Source: SEC Form 17-A (2024)

## Company: STI Education Systems Holdings, Inc. (STI)
Sector: Services / Education
STI Education Systems Holdings, Inc. (STI), formerly JTH Davies Holdings, Inc., was originally established in 1928 as the Philippine branch office of Theo H. Davies & Co., a Hawaiian corporation. The Company was reincorporated as a Philippine corporation registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on June 28, 1946. After many years of operations as part of the Jardine-Matheson group, STI was sold to local Philippine investors in 2006. In March 2010, the Company became part of the Tanco Group of Companies. On September 10, 2012, the SEC approved the change in name to the present one.

STI is the holding company within the Tanco Group that derives investment in its education business. The Company's subsidiaries are STI Education Services Group, Inc. (STI ESG); STI West Negros University, Inc.; iACADEMY, Inc.; and Attenborough Holdings Corporation. STI ESG has a total of 63 schools nationwide.

storedThesis:
STI Education Systems Holdings is a straightforward business to understand: it operates the Philippines' largest network of private vocational and technical schools, with 63 STI campuses nationwide plus iACADEMY and STI West Negros University under the Tanco Group umbrella. The value proposition is clear — affordable, employment-oriented tertiary education targeting middle-income Filipino families who cannot afford elite universities but want a credential with real job-market relevance. This is a business a sensible investor can follow, and the demand driver (economic mobility through education) is durable across most macro cycles.

The moat is real but not exceptional. STI's scale — 132,000+ enrolled students across 63 schools — confers a cost and brand advantage that a new entrant cannot easily replicate. Students enrolled in multi-year programs face meaningful switching costs (credit transfer friction, lost time). The vocational-tech positioning also creates some regulatory moat, as CHED accreditation for new programs is slow and bureaucratic. What weakens the moat is that the product is not truly differentiated at the premium end: STI competes on price and accessibility, not prestige, which makes it vulnerable to public school expansion and competing private chains. The Forbes Asia Best Under a Billion recognition (2025) suggests the market sees execution quality, but this is not a Jollibee-level brand fortress.

Management under Eusebio Tanco has operated with discipline: debt/equity at 0.19x is conservative for an education company with fixed-cost campuses, regular dividends have been maintained, and the 38% net income jump to ₱2.22B in FY2024-2025 reflects genuine operating leverage rather than financial engineering. Importantly, when the Middle East crisis began pressuring OFW remittances and driving dropout risk in early 2026, management disclosed the enrollment headwind proactively rather than burying it — that matters in a market where disclosure culture is spotty. However, the Tanco family's control structure warrants ongoing scrutiny for related-party transactions that could disadvantage minority shareholders, which is a standard governance risk in Philippine conglomerates.

The valuation case is compelling even without a formal Rule #1 sticker price. At ₱1.22, STI trades at 5.5x earnings and 1.0x book, with a 3.7% dividend yield — pricing that implies the market expects earnings stagnation or deterioration. The 16.2% ROIC and 51.9% FCF growth over the measured period tell a very different story: this is a capital-efficient business generating significant free cash that management is returning to shareholders. The near-term enrollment headwind is real — total enrollment slipped to 132,941 from 139,155 in SY2025-2026, driven partly by OFW remittance pressure and partly by the earlier start of public school classes pulling junior/senior high students. Critically, tertiary enrollment (the higher-margin CHED-regulated segment) actually grew 14% to 73,421 continuing students, suggesting the core college business is holding and that the headline enrollment decline overstates the revenue impact. Ongoing Middle East instability is the key watch item: a prolonged OFW income shock could compress new enrollments for multiple school years, which would pressure revenue growth even if margins hold.

At current prices, STI offers a margin of safety that is difficult to ignore on fundamentals alone — P/E of 5.5x with double-digit ROIC is the kind of gap between price and value that Rule #1 seeks. The business is meaningful, the moat is adequate, management is credible, and the price is clearly below any reasonable estimate of intrinsic value. The reservation is macro: the OFW remittance story is unresolved, and Philippine private education faces a structural pressure as public school capacity expands. Watch for Q1 SY2026-2027 enrollment data (typically released August-September 2026) — stabilization there would convert this from a watch to a conviction buy. At the current price, this is a watch with a strong lean toward accumulation on any further weakness below ₱1.10.
